meta.title: Bug Hunt Bench
meta.subtitle: 105 real bugs hidden in two production repos. Frontier coding models find and fix what they can, graded blind.
meta.author: Pawel Huryn

method: Two unrelated production codebases: a ~28K-line TypeScript VS Code extension (45 bugs) and a ~60K-line React/Supabase LMS (60 bugs). Most bugs are real regressions reverted from the repos' own fix history, each with its fix commit.
The test suites stay green, so nothing points at the answers. Every model gets the identical prompt, one round per repo, in its own native agentic CLI.
Grading is blind: the model's diff is the ground truth, not its report. An independent judge scores against a withheld answer key and never learns which model produced the diff.

The score counts planted bugs only. Some models bug-max - they report a long list of real but irrelevant problems, and that list has no answer key and no ceiling, so counting it would just reward volume. Unplanted fixes are tracked separately and never scored.

glossary.fixed: Planted bugs fixed and verified against the withheld answer key. The only number in the score.
glossary.partial: The defect was addressed but not fully closed. Not counted in the score.
glossary.claimed_only: Named in the model's report but not fixed in its diff - including bugs it saw and chose not to touch. Not counted in the score.
glossary.extras: A real defect the model fixed that nobody planted. Genuine work - but the set has no answer key and no ceiling, so it cannot be scored reliably. Counted, never added to the score.
glossary.cost_bill: An actual invoice or credits delta.
glossary.cost_list: A token-count estimate at published list rates, not a bill.
glossary.cost_floor: Reconstructed lower bound - this CLI reports context occupancy, not billing.
glossary.cost_free: Served free at the time of the run.
glossary.effort_verified_ceiling: This model's highest reasoning setting. We checked that changing the setting actually changes what the model does.
glossary.effort_verified: We checked that changing this reasoning setting actually changes what the model does.
glossary.effort_first_party: A setting the vendor documents in their own tool. Taken at face value, not separately tested.
glossary.effort_clamped: We asked for a higher setting and the tool quietly ran a lower one. Published as a correction.
glossary.effort_inert_default: This route ignores the effort setting entirely, so the model ran at its own default. There was no working dial to turn.

caveats: One round per model per repo. Same-setting variance is real and measured: three Grok 4.5 runs on identical settings scored 16, 13 and 17.

Wall clock is the same measure on every row: repo 1 plus repo 2 agent time, with dependency install and health checks excluded. Two things bend it, and both are marked on the score-and-time map. Three runs took their two repo legs concurrently - the sum is still like-for-like, but two agents sharing one machine and one API key contend, so those figures can run high rather than low. And one figure is adjusted: the retired-Gemini-CLI run excludes a 35-minute harness stall, the only number here that is not what the harness measured.

Cost is not one kind of number: some figures are an actual bill, some are a token-count estimate at published list rates, one CLI only allows a reconstructed lower bound, and one run was free. The key under the board names which is which - they are not interchangeable, and none of them is a quote for what you would pay.
39 of the 105 bugs have survived every model in every run to date. The count moves as new runs land: it fell from 49 to 44 during the 27-28 August waves.

runs.caveat: The endpoint deserializer also accepts an undocumented `ultra`, which DeepSeek own docs never mention (they give none|low|high|max, default high). Sampled n=4 it straddles both high and max and resolves to neither, and nothing in that sample exceeds max band - so `max` is the top of the documented dial and nothing measured reasons more than it, which is what the ceiling label claims. Which tier `ultra` aliases is unresolved and left that way rather than guessed.
runs.note: DeepSeek newest Flash generation, benchmarked on DeepSeek OWN Anthropic-compatible API - no aggregator, no proxy. Claude Code puts --effort on the wire as output_config.effort; the endpoint 400-rejects an invented tier and names its enum, and a thinking-volume sweep separates the tiers with DISJOINT ranges (high mean 30.5K chars, max mean 83.6K, n=3), so max was applied and not merely requested. Cost is a real bill, not an estimate: DeepSeek sells prepaid credit, so each leg is charged at the balance drop across it. $1.08 of real credit for 24/105 - the same score as Fable 5 and as Opus 5 at medium. Those two are list estimates and this is a bill, so read the gap as an order of magnitude and not as a ratio.

One run per tier. A single non-monotonic point is a finding about this run, not a demonstrated property of the medium tier - the board's own variance evidence (three Grok 4.5 runs at one setting scoring 16, 13 and 17) is the reason that distinction is enforced here. What the row does establish is that the shell-first strategy and the low score arrived together, which is a mechanism worth having on record either way.
runs.note: Fable 5.1's dial does not run in a straight line: medium scores 21/105, BELOW its own low row (29) and well below high (33) and max (43). The run is clean - both legs exited success, no truncation, no permission denials, no tool errors - and the raw captures say why in the tool mix rather than in the thinking. At medium the model worked almost entirely through the shell: 83 Bash calls against 3 Reads and ZERO Edits or Greps on repo 1, and 99 Bash against 2 Reads and zero Edits on repo 2. At low it read the codebase instead - 44 Reads, 20 Greps, 16 Edits on repo 1. That shows up in the billing shape too: medium pulled 4.0M cached-read tokens on repo 1 against low's 19.7M, because a session that never reads files into context keeps a small context to re-send. Fewer bugs found is what you would expect from a model that barely looked at the code.

runs.caveat: The honesty profile is worse at this tier than at max, which is the opposite of the usual direction: 3 partials and 2 claimed-only here against 0 and 0 at max. At n=1 per tier that is a difference of a handful of bugs, not a demonstrated property of the tier.
runs.note: The dial companion to the max row: same model, same first-party endpoint, same day, one tier down. It costs 5 strict fixes (19/105 against 24) and every one of them is on repo 1 - 9/45 against 14/45, while repo 2 lands on exactly the same 10/60. The tier is doing visibly less work for that: 26.1 min against 42.6, 160K output tokens against 240K, 57M cached reads against 82M, $0.31 against $1.08. high is DeepSeek's documented default, but it is requested explicitly here rather than left implicit, because on this endpoint the omitted field measured as neither high nor max.

Run as the behavioural control for the Ox Alpha stealth slug, whose wire fingerprint matches this model's serving stack. Their claim lists overlapped heavily, but only 10 of their 25 graded fixes are the same bugs.

Tencent Hunyuan 4 preview (MoE, 49B active of 770B), benchmarked day-one via OpenRouter. This is the model's ceiling. Tencent documents reasoning_effort as a BINARY switch - `high` (the default, which is what ran here) or `no_think` - so there is no higher tier to request and no graded scale to climb. 18/105 for $3.13 real OpenRouter bill. On repo 1 it claimed 10 fixes and 9 verified against the answer key. Single host (Tencent Cloud); day-one 429/404s absorbed by proxy retries.

runs.caveat: Two honest limits on this row. (1) The effort label is `first_party`, not `verified`: a high-vs-max thinking sweep on Pro itself came out INCONCLUSIVE at n=3 - means 51.1K vs 85.1K characters, but between-level 1.66x against a worst within-level spread of 1.78x, with the ranges overlapping. The same sweep on V4.1 Flash the same hour was cleanly disjoint, which is why the Flash rows carry `verified` and this one does not. The path-level facts still hold: the endpoint 400-rejects an invented tier, and the served model id was read back as V4-Pro on every gate call. (2) The $1.89 is a real credits delta for the ARM; the per-repo split is that bill allocated by each leg's token value at list, because a runner bug read the wrong meter for the individual legs. Both metrics rows say so.
runs.note: The board's first look at DeepSeek's Pro model with an effort dial in front of it. The existing V4-Pro row (Aug 1) ran through OpenRouter at an inert default; this one runs on DeepSeek's own Anthropic-compatible endpoint at an explicitly requested max. It scores 16/105 - better than that row's 10, and well under the V4.1 Flash rows that cost a fraction of it. On this bench the newer Flash generation beats the older Pro flagship at every tier tried: Flash max 24 and Flash high 19 against Pro max 16, at $1.08 and $0.31 against $1.89. Pro is also the slower model here, 37.2 min against Flash max's 42.6 only because it wrote less.

runs.superseded: One of three runs at the same setting (16 / 13 / 17) - the spread is this board's variance evidence.

runs.note: The named release of the Ox Alpha stealth slug, run on Z.ai's own host with provider fallbacks off. 13 against the stealth run's 16 is inside this board's same-setting spread. The bill is at the 50% launch price; list doubles after 9 Sep 2026. Its five claimed-only are bugs it named in its report and deliberately left alone.

runs.caveat: Two things to keep in view. (1) The effort label is `first_party`, not `verified`, for the same reason as the max row: a high-vs-max thinking sweep on Pro itself never separated - at n=5 the between-level ratio is 1.35x against a worst within-level spread of 2.27x, with the ranges overlapping heavily. The path-level facts do hold - the endpoint 400-rejects an invented tier and names its enum, and the served model read back as V4-Pro on every gate call. This bench pair is a second and coarser reading of the same question, and it does land in the expected direction (16 at max, 13 at high, with more extras and more money at max) - but it is n=1 per tier on 105 bugs, so it corroborates the dial rather than proving it. (2) This arm was run twice. The first attempt was VOIDED, not scored: a machine-wide tool hook on the bench host pointed at a moved script and denied every tool call the model made, so it diagnosed a broken environment, wrote no report, changed no file, and exited 0 after 160 seconds - a clean-looking row for a leg in which nothing happened. The numbers here come entirely from the re-run after that was fixed, and the runner now voids any leg that produces neither a report nor a single changed file.
runs.note: The dial companion to the Pro max row: same model, same first-party endpoint, same hour, one tier down. It costs 3 strict fixes - 13/105 against 16 - and saves $0.81, $1.08 against $1.89, on 26.6 minutes against 37.2. It also moves where the score comes from: max is even across the two repos (8/45 and 8/60) while high collapses on repo 1 to 4/45 and edges ahead on repo 2 at 9/60. The unplanted-extras column tracks the money rather than the score - 4 genuine extras at max, 1 at high. high is DeepSeek's documented default; it is requested explicitly here rather than left implicit, because on this endpoint an omitted field measured as neither tier.
